lead: This unit studies maps between vector spaces that respect vector addition and scalar multiplication. You learn to compute kernels, ranges, ranks and nullities, to write a linear map as a matrix, and to change basis. You also meet invertible maps and dual spaces.
about: The unit begins with the definition and first examples of a linear map in 3.1, including composition and linear operators. Chapter 3.2 defines the kernel and range, the two subspaces that describe what a map loses and what it produces. Chapter 3.3 proves the rank-nullity theorem, the counting rule dim V = rank T + nullity T. Chapter 3.4 writes a map as a matrix and explains change of basis. Chapter 3.5, advanced and taught in only a few universities, covers invertible maps and isomorphisms. Chapter 3.6, also advanced, introduces linear functionals and the dual space. The examples use small matrices over R so you can check every step.

chapters.idea: A linear map is a function between vector spaces that preserves addition and scalar multiplication.
chapters.depth: Definition T: V → W over a field F, usually R or C; the two rules T(u + v) = T(u) + T(v) and T(cu) = cT(u); examples: zero map, identity map, scaling, rotation, derivative on polynomials, and x ↦ Ax; non-examples such as T(x, y) = (x + 1, y) and T(x) = x². Define linear operator as a linear map V → V. Show composition of linear maps is linear. Some syllabi call these linear maps or linear transformations. Keep proofs to one line; do not compute kernels or matrices here.

figure.title: Additivity check
figure.aria: A flow diagram sends u and v through addition then T, and separately through T then addition, meeting at a node that says the two results must be equal.

chapters.example: Define T: R² → R² by T(x, y) = (2x + y, x − 3y). (a) Show T is linear. (b) Find T(1, 2). (c) Find T(e₁) and T(e₂), where e₁ = (1, 0), e₂ = (0, 1). Answer: T(1, 2) = (4, −5); T(e₁) = (2, 1), T(e₂) = (1, −3); expand T((x, y) + (x′, y′)) and T(c(x, y)) to check both rules.
chapters.trap: T(0) must be 0, so a map with a constant shift like T(x, y) = (x + 1, y) is not linear. Test both rules: a map can look harmless and still fail scaling.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2: vector spaces, subspaces, linear combinations.
chapters.leave: Kernel, range and matrix representation belong to chapters 3.2–3.4; eigenvalues belong to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: The kernel collects inputs that map to zero, and the range collects all outputs.
chapters.depth: Kernel, also called null space: ker T = {v in V : T(v) = 0}. Range, also called image: im T = {T(v) : v in V}. Prove both are subspaces. Give the test for injectivity: T is one-to-one iff ker T = {0}. Give the test for surjectivity: T is onto iff im T = W. Find bases from equations and from a matrix. Use the words null space and image, which some syllabi prefer. Do not prove rank-nullity yet.

figure.title: Kernel and range of T
figure.aria: A diagram splits the domain V into the kernel, which maps to zero, and the remaining vectors, whose images fill the range inside W.

chapters.example: Let T: R³ → R² be T(x, y, z) = (x + 2y − z, 2x + 4y − 2z). Find a basis for ker T and for range T, and state nullity and rank. Answer: ker T = span{(1, 0, 1), (0, 1, 2)}, nullity 2; range T = span{(1, 2)}, rank 1.
chapters.trap: The kernel always contains 0, so it is never empty. The range is a subspace of W, not all of W unless T is onto. Do not solve T(v) = w when the question asks for ker T.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.1; Unit 2: subspaces, span and basis.
chapters.leave: The rank-nullity proof is chapter 3.3; matrix rank algorithms are in Unit 1.

chapters.idea: For a linear map on a finite-dimensional space, dim V = rank T + nullity T.
chapters.depth: Define rank T = dim(im T) and nullity T = dim(ker T). Prove the theorem by taking a basis of ker T and extending it to a basis of V. Corollaries: T is injective iff rank T = dim V; if dim V = dim W, then injective, surjective and bijective are equivalent. Some syllabi call this the dimension theorem or Sylvester's law of nullity. Apply it to matrices by counting pivots and free variables. Keep the proof short and finite-dimensional.

figure.title: Counting a basis of V
figure.aria: A basis of V is split into k vectors that lie in the kernel and n − k vectors whose images form a basis of the range, so n = k + (n − k).

chapters.example: Let T: R⁴ → R³ be T(x₁, x₂, x₃, x₄) = (x₁ + x₂, x₃, x₄ − x₂). Find rank T and nullity T, and verify the rank-nullity theorem. Answer: ker T = span{(−1, 1, 0, 1)}, nullity 1; rank T = 3; 4 = 3 + 1.
chapters.trap: The theorem needs V finite-dimensional. rank T is dim(range T), not the number of rows of a matrix. nullity is dim(ker T), not the number of zero columns.
chapters.leave: Eigenvalues and diagonalization are in Unit 4; row-reduction practice is in Unit 1.

chapters.idea: A linear map is stored in a matrix once you choose bases, and changing basis changes the matrix by conjugation.
chapters.depth: Coordinate vector [v]_B. Matrix [T]_C←B whose j-th column is [T(b_j)]_C. Formula [T(v)]_C = [T]_C←B [v]_B. Change-of-basis matrix P from B to the standard basis, and the similarity formula [T]_B = P⁻¹ A P when domain and codomain use the same basis. Work 2×2 examples with integer entries. Some syllabi say matrix representation of a linear transformation. Do not diagonalize; that is Unit 4.

figure.title: Columns of [T]_B for B = {(1,1), (1,2)}
figure.aria: A two-row array shows the two columns of the matrix of T in basis B: the first column is (8, −5) and the second is (13, −9).

chapters.example: For T(x, y) = (2x + y, x − 3y) and B = {(1, 1), (1, 2)}, find [T]_B. Check with P = [[1, 1], [1, 2]]. Answer: [T]_B = [[8, 13], [−5, −9]], and P⁻¹ A P gives the same matrix with A = [[2, 1], [1, −3]].
chapters.trap: Basis order matters. Domain basis and codomain basis can differ. The formula is [T]_C←B = C⁻¹ A B, not B⁻¹ A C.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 3.1–3.3; Unit 1: matrix multiplication; Unit 2: basis and coordinates.
chapters.leave: Similar matrices and diagonalization are in Unit 4; determinants are in Unit 1 or Unit 4.

chapters.idea: An invertible linear map is a bijection with a linear inverse, and two spaces are isomorphic when such a map exists.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this chapter. Definition: T is invertible if there is T⁻¹: W → V with T⁻¹T = I_V and TT⁻¹ = I_W. Equivalently T is bijective. Show T⁻¹ is linear. For finite-dimensional V and W, T is invertible iff dim V = dim W and ker T = {0}; its matrix is square with nonzero determinant. Define isomorphism and isomorphic spaces. Some syllabi say non-singular linear transformation. Prove the inverse is linear and give a 2×2 example. Keep it short.

figure.title: Inverse map
figure.aria: A loop diagram shows T taking V to W bijectively and T inverse taking W back to V.

chapters.example: Let T: R² → R² be T(x, y) = (2x + y, x − 3y). Show T is invertible and find T⁻¹(1, 0). Answer: det A = −7 ≠ 0, so T is invertible; T⁻¹(1, 0) = (3/7, 1/7).
chapters.trap: A linear map can be one-to-one without being onto unless dim V = dim W. A square matrix with determinant 0 is not invertible. Do not call a map invertible just because you can solve one equation.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 3.1–3.4; Unit 1: invertible matrices and determinants.
chapters.leave: Determinant computation is in Unit 1; diagonalization is in Unit 4.

chapters.idea: A linear functional is a linear map to the field, and the dual space collects all such functionals.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this chapter. Linear functional: a linear map f: V → F. Dual space V* = set of all linear functionals with pointwise addition and scaling. Dual basis f₁, …, f_n to a basis b₁, …, b_n: f_i(b_j) = δ_ij. Show every functional is a coordinate sum. Mention the double dual V** briefly. Some syllabi say linear form. Keep to finite dimensions; do not use inner products.

figure.title: A functional lands in the field
figure.aria: A diagram shows a functional f taking vectors from V to scalars in F, while the dual space V* collects all such functionals.

chapters.example: Let V = R² and f(x, y) = 3x − 2y. (a) Show f is a linear functional. (b) For B = {(1, 1), (1, −1)}, find the dual basis f₁, f₂. Answer: f(1, 4) = −5; f₁(x, y) = (x + y)/2, f₂(x, y) = (x − y)/2, and f_i(b_j) = δ_ij.
chapters.trap: A functional is a map to scalars, not a vector. The dual basis depends on the order of the original basis. Do not confuse V* with V.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 3.1 and 3.4; Unit 2: basis and coordinates.
chapters.leave: Inner product spaces and Riesz representation are in Unit 5; annihilators are for a more advanced course.
